newsitem.title: UK: Europe returns to haunt Major in poll battle.
newsitem.headline: Europe returns to haunt Major in poll battle.

text.p: Europe, the issue which has repeatedly frustrated Prime Minister John Major's efforts to present his Conservative Party as united, returned to haunt him on Friday, 20 days before the May 1 election.

With polls showing Major set to suffer a humiliating defeat, the opposition Labour Party pounced gleefully on allegations that a junior minister had defied Major's authority on the vexed issue of the single European currency.

Labour leader Tony Blair, launching his party's business manifesto, said Major should either force agriculture minister Angela Browning to withdraw an election newsletter in which she spoke out against the single currency, or sack her.
"This morning we see what business dislikes most -- a government weakly led and divided, disorganised and disintegrating over its central policy on Europe," Blair said.

Almost a third of all Conservative candidates are expected to ignore Major's "wait and see" stance on the single currency in their personal election addresses and tell local electors that they could never vote to jettison the pound sterling.
But rebellion by rank-and-file candidates is viewed as less serious than a departure from the official line by a member of Major's government.

The Times newspaper quoted a newsletter issued by Browning to her constituents in Devon, south-west England, as saying that if Britain joined a single currency, it would have to hand over foreign currency reserves to a new European central bank.
The consequence would be "the end of sovereignty of the nation state, and if that is what is offered I have made it very clear that I will not support it."
Major denied Browning had stepped out of line, saying that she had made it clear "her views are entirely compatible with the government and the (Conservative) manifesto."

Labour, buoyed by two opinion polls putting it 22 points ahead, claimed a crucial breakthrough by at last winning the trust of Britain's business community which in the past has overwhelmingly supported the Conservatives.

The party has jettisoned its previous socialist philosophy and pledged in its business manifesto to promote stable low-inflationary economic growth, to keep government spending low and avoid burdensome regulation of business.
"Far from being in conflict, the interests of the Labour Party and the business community are in harmony," economics spokesman Gordon Brown wrote in a foreword to the manifesto.
"To bring about the fair and prosperous society that Labour seeks, we need successful and enterprising businesses making strong profits."

The manifesto launch featured business people proclaiming they intended to break the habit of a lifetime and vote Labour. "We have a lot of support among the business community in a way that was unimaginable a few years ago," Blair said.

"Business can do business with new Labour. That in my view is one of the healthiest changes in British politics for a very long time," said Gerry Robinson, chief executive of leisure and media group Granada.
